amt-amc-practice-1-jun-01.title: Use a fraction
amt-amc-practice-1-jun-01.body:
$0.04=\frac{4}{100}=\frac1{25}$, and dividing by $\frac1{25}$ is the same as multiplying by $25$. So $\frac1{0.04}=25$.

**Answer: (C) 25**

amt-amc-practice-1-jun-02.title: Find the numbers
amt-amc-practice-1-jun-02.body:
The smallest three are consecutive with average $60\div3=20$, so they are $19, 20, 21$. The five cards are $19,20,21,22,23$, and the largest three add up to $21+22+23=66$.

**Answer: (E) 66**

amt-amc-practice-1-jun-02.title: Shift by two
amt-amc-practice-1-jun-02.body:
The largest three numbers are the smallest three numbers each moved up by $2$ places (1st $\to$ 3rd, 2nd $\to$ 4th, 3rd $\to$ 5th), so each is $2$ more. Their sum is $60+3\times2=66$.

**Answer: (E) 66**

amt-amc-practice-1-jun-03.title: Use a triangular grid
amt-amc-practice-1-jun-03.body:
The shortest length in the figure is half the side of a shaded triangle. Use it to draw a triangular grid: each shaded triangle has side $2$ units and the large triangle has side $5$ units (along the bottom: shaded $2$, gap $1$, shaded $2$).

A triangle of side $n$ units is made of $n^2$ unit triangles. So each shaded triangle has $4$ unit triangles and the large one has $25$. The shaded part is $4\times4=16$ of the $25$ unit triangles: $\frac{16}{25}$.

**Answer: (E) $\frac{16}{25}$**

amt-amc-practice-1-jun-03.title: Similar triangles
amt-amc-practice-1-jun-03.body:
Let a small triangle have side $2$. Along the bottom of the large triangle there are two small triangles with a gap between them; the gap is the base of an inverted triangle whose side equals half a small side, i.e. $1$ (the centre triangle sits on top of it with the corners touching). So the large triangle has side $2+1+2=5$.

Areas of equilateral triangles scale as the square of the side, so the four small triangles cover
$$\frac{4\times2^2}{5^2}=\frac{16}{25}$$
of the large triangle.

**Answer: (E) $\frac{16}{25}$**

amt-amc-practice-1-jun-04.title: List them by direction
amt-amc-practice-1-jun-04.body:
A segment passes through exactly one other dot when that dot is its midpoint, i.e. when it jumps "two steps" in the grid.

* Horizontal (length $2$ along a row of $5$): $3$ per row, $3$ rows: $9$.
* Vertical (from top row to bottom row): $5$.
* At $45^\circ$ (two steps across and two down, in either diagonal direction): $3+3=6$.
* Others (four across and two down, through the centre dot of each half): $2$.

Total $9+5+6+2=22$.

**Answer: (C) 22**

amt-amc-practice-1-jun-04.title: Count by the middle dot
amt-amc-practice-1-jun-04.body:
Each such segment has a unique middle dot, and the segment is determined by its middle dot $M$ and one end $E$ (the other end is the reflection of $E$ in $M$, which must also be a dot). So for each dot count the pairs of dots symmetric about it:
* Dots on the top and bottom rows: no dot has a partner on the "other side" vertically, and along the row only the three middle dots have one horizontal pair each: $3+3=6$.
* Middle row: the two end dots have $1$ (the vertical pair) each; the dots in positions $2$ and $4$ have $4$ each (vertical, horizontal, two diagonals); the centre dot has $6$.

Total $6+1+1+4+4+6=22$.

**Answer: (C) 22**

amt-amc-practice-1-jun-05.title: Count all, then subtract clashes
Go jacket by jacket
amt-amc-practice-1-jun-05.body:
* **Black jacket:** any shirt with any trousers except the same colour: shirts white, blue, red, yellow with trousers brown/white/yellow: $3+3+3+3=12$, minus white–white and yellow–yellow: $10$.
* **Brown jacket:** trousers can't be brown, so white or yellow; with $4$ shirts that's $8$, minus white–white and yellow–yellow: $6$.
* **Blue jacket:** shirt can't be blue: white, red or yellow, with $3$ trousers: $9$, minus white–white and yellow–yellow: $7$.

Total $10+6+7=23$.

**Answer: (A) 23**

amt-amc-practice-1-jun-06.title: Rectangles are pairs of diameters
amt-amc-practice-1-jun-06.body:
A rectangle inscribed in a circle has its diagonals as diameters, so its four corners are the ends of two diameters. The $18$ points form $9$ diametrically opposite pairs, and we get a rectangle exactly when two of these pairs are chosen completely.

* $10$ points are not enough: choose $10$ consecutive points. These contain both ends of only one diameter (the first and the tenth point), so no rectangle.
* $11$ points are enough: if at most one pair were complete, then at most $1\cdot2 + 8\cdot1 = 10$ points could be chosen (two from one pair, one from each of the other $8$). So with $11$ points, at least two pairs are complete, giving a rectangle.

**Answer: 11**

amt-amc-practice-1-jun-06.title: Pigeonhole on the 9 diameters
amt-amc-practice-1-jun-06.body:
Think of the $9$ diameters as boxes, each holding $2$ points. Choosing $k$ points puts them into the boxes; a rectangle appears when $2$ boxes are full.

The most points you can choose with at most one full box is $2+1\times8 = 10$ (fill one box and take one point from each other box) — for example $10$ consecutive points. Any $11$th point fills a second box. So the minimum number that guarantees a rectangle is $11$.

**Answer: 11**
